prompt: A sample of 64 deliveries has a standard deviation of 12 minutes. What is the standard error of the mean, in minutes?
A report gives 'mean basket R$ 82.39 ± 79.86'. Assuming the ± is the standard deviation, what does it tell you?

choices.text: That the true mean is between R$ 2.53 and R$ 162.25
choices.why: The standard deviation describes the baskets, not the uncertainty of the mean.

choices.text: That individual baskets vary widely
choices.why: Right. The uncertainty of the mean is the standard error, R$ 12.63 for 40 baskets.

choices.text: That the mean is known to within R$ 79.86
choices.why: That would be the standard error's job, and it is much smaller.

choices.text: That the sample was too small to trust
choices.why: The standard deviation says nothing about sample size; it would be just as large with 4,000 baskets.

prompt: Horta quadruples its sample from 40 to 160 baskets. What happens to the standard deviation and the standard error?
hint: Which one describes the data, and which the estimate?

choices.text: Both halve
choices.why: The standard deviation describes the baskets, which are as varied as ever.

choices.text: The standard deviation halves; the standard error stays
choices.why: It is the other way round.

choices.text: Both stay the same
choices.why: The standard error falls with √n.

choices.text: Standard error halves, the other stays
choices.why: Right. Four times the data, half the uncertainty about the mean; the baskets themselves vary as much as before.

prompt: A sample mean is 50 with a standard error of 4. Using 1.96, what is the upper end of the 95% confidence interval? Give two decimal places.
Moving from a 95% to a 99% confidence interval, on the same data, does what to the interval?

choices.text: Widens it
choices.why: Right. More confidence needs a larger multiplier: 2.576 instead of 1.96.

choices.text: Narrows it, as the estimate is now more certain
choices.why: The data has not changed; asking to be right more often costs width.

choices.text: Shifts it towards the true mean
choices.why: The centre stays at the sample mean; only the width changes.

choices.text: Leaves it unchanged, since the standard error is the same
choices.why: The standard error is the same, but the multiplier is not.

prompt: A 95% confidence interval comes from a convenience sample of the 60 deliveries nearest the warehouse. What does it describe?
hint: What can an interval correct, and what can it not?

choices.text: The mean of all of Horta's deliveries, with 95% confidence
choices.why: The interval inherits the sample's bias; it is centred on the near routes, not on all deliveries.

choices.text: Nothing, as confidence intervals need 100 or more values
choices.why: Sixty is plenty for an interval; the problem is which sixty.

choices.text: At best, deliveries on the near routes
choices.why: Right. A confidence interval accounts for random wobble, never for bias; it is a precise statement about the wrong population.

choices.text: The mean of the far routes, by symmetry
choices.why: There is no such symmetry; the far routes were not sampled.

prompt: Which reading of a 95% confidence interval is correct?
hint: What is random: the true mean or the interval?

choices.text: There is a 95% chance the true mean is inside this interval
choices.why: The true mean is fixed; this interval either contains it or not. The 95% belongs to the method.

choices.text: 95% of the data lies inside the interval
choices.why: The interval is about the mean, not about individual values; most baskets lie outside a narrow interval.

choices.text: 95% of intervals built this way contain the true mean
choices.why: Right. Repeat the sampling many times and about 95% of the intervals catch the truth.

choices.text: The sample mean is correct to within 95%
choices.why: That phrase has no meaning; the confidence level is not a margin.

prompt: If 100 researchers each draw a random sample and build a correct 95% interval, about how many intervals miss the true mean?
Over 1,000 samples of 40 baskets, the 95% intervals contained the true mean 94.3% of the time. Why not exactly 95%?
hint: Which assumption is weakest for these baskets?

choices.text: The baskets are skewed, so 40 is not quite enough
choices.why: Right. The normal approximation to the sample mean is not yet exact for such skewed data, so coverage falls a little short.

choices.text: The intervals were computed wrongly
choices.why: They used the right formula; the approximation behind it is what is imperfect here.

choices.text: A 95% interval only promises 94%
choices.why: It promises 95% when its assumptions hold.

choices.text: The true mean changed during the simulation
choices.why: The population, and its mean, were fixed throughout.

prompt: A sample of 10 has mean 20 and standard deviation 3. With the t multiplier 2.262 for 9 degrees of freedom, what is the margin of the 95% interval? Give two decimal places.
Why does a 95% interval from 8 observations use 2.36 instead of 1.96?
hint: What was estimated that the normal curve assumes is known?

choices.text: Because 8 observations are always skewed
choices.why: Skew is not the reason; the estimated standard deviation is.

choices.text: Small samples need 99% confidence
choices.why: The confidence level is still 95%; only the distribution changes.

choices.text: To make the interval narrower
choices.why: A larger multiplier makes it wider.

choices.text: s was estimated from few values
choices.why: Right. The t distribution's thicker tails pay for the uncertainty in s.

prompt: Match each number of degrees of freedom to its 95% t multiplier.
hint: Fewer degrees of freedom, larger multiplier.

prompt: Gosset signed his 1908 paper on the t distribution with the pen name ___.
hint: The distribution is still called by it.

prompt: In a survey of 400 customers, 248 are satisfied. What is the margin of the 95% interval, in percentage points? Give one decimal place.
Why should the usual formula not be used for a proportion from Horta's twelve orders, of which three were late?
hint: Count the yeses and the noes.

choices.text: Proportions cannot have confidence intervals
choices.why: They can; the issue is this formula with these counts.

choices.text: Three late is far below the 10 each side it needs
choices.why: Right. With so few, the normal approximation fails; a Wilson interval suits small counts.

choices.text: Twelve orders are a population, not a sample
choices.why: They are a sample of Horta's orders; the problem is size.

choices.text: The share late, 0.25, is too far from 0.5
choices.why: 0.25 is fine with enough data; the counts are the problem.

prompt: Using the worst case p = 0.5, how many people does a survey need for a 95% margin of 4 percentage points? Give a whole number, rounded up.
A planned survey of 535 orders gives a margin of about R$ 5 on the mean basket. What sample would give R$ 2.50?

choices.text: About 1,070
choices.why: Doubling the sample divides the margin by about 1.41, not by 2.

choices.text: About 2,140
choices.why: Right. Halving the margin needs four times the sample.

choices.text: About 800
choices.why: That reduces the margin by less than a fifth.

choices.text: About 268, half as many
choices.why: Fewer orders make the margin wider, not narrower.

prompt: Put the steps of building a 95% interval for a mean from one sample in order.
hint: The interval is the last thing built.
items: Compute the sample mean and standard deviation
Divide the standard deviation by √n to get the standard error
Find the t multiplier for n − 1 degrees of freedom
Add and subtract multiplier × standard error from the mean
